pages.text: The Iliad: Selected Episodes

image.note: Cover: Greek ships and the high walls of Troy

pages.text: Contents. The Quarrel / The War Without Achilles / Patroclus / The Wrath / Achilles and Hector / Priam and Achilles.

Three thousand years ago, a poet named Homer told of a great war: how the Greeks sailed to the city of Troy, and fought for ten long years, and of the gods who took sides above them. This is not the whole tale, but its beating heart: the anger of one great warrior, Achilles.

image.note: Greek ships drawn up before Troy

pages.text: For nine years the Greek army had camped on the shore below the high walls of Troy, and still the city stood. The mightiest of all the Greek warriors was Achilles, so strong and so swift that no man could stand against him. But this is the story of how his own anger nearly lost the war.

image.note: The Greek camp below Troy's walls

pages.text: It began with a quarrel. Agamemnon, the proud commander of all the Greeks, took from Achilles a prize that was rightly his, simply because he could. Achilles was blind with fury. "You take what I won," he said. "Then fight your war without me."

image.note: Achilles and Agamemnon face to face, furious

pages.text: And Achilles did just that. He and his loyal soldiers withdrew to their ships and would not fight. His mother was a sea-goddess, and he begged her to let the Greeks feel his loss. So the greatest warrior sat idle by the sea, nursing his anger, while his own side marched out without him.

image.note: Achilles brooding alone by his ships

pages.text: Without Achilles, the Greeks began to lose. High on Mount Olympus the gods watched, and took sides, some for the Greeks, some for Troy, meddling in the battle below as if it were a game. An arrow guided here, a warrior hidden in mist there. Mortals fought, and gods pulled the strings.

image.note: The gods on Olympus watching the battle

pages.text: Inside the city, Troy's greatest champion made ready: Hector, brave and noble, the finest of all the Trojans, and the one man who might match Achilles. Before he went to fight, Hector climbed to say farewell to his wife, Andromache, and their baby son.

image.note: Hector arming, the city behind him

pages.text: Andromache begged him to stay. "You are husband and father and brother to me, all at once," she wept. "Do not make me a widow." Hector held her, and reached for his little son, but the baby cried, frightened by the great horsehair crest on his father's helmet.

image.note: Hector reaching for his baby, tall helmet plume

pages.text: So Hector laughed, gently, and lifted off the shining helmet, and only then would his son come to him. He kissed the child, and held his wife, and spoke softly. "I must go. But whatever comes, know that I loved you." Then he set the helmet back on, and went out to war.

image.note: Hector kissing his son, helmet set aside

pages.text: As the Greeks were driven back to their very ships, one man could bear it no longer: Patroclus, the dearest friend Achilles had in all the world. "If you will not fight," he begged, "then lend me your armour. Let the Trojans think you have returned, and take fresh heart to our side."

image.note: Patroclus pleading with Achilles

pages.text: Achilles, still too proud to fight himself, agreed. Patroclus put on the famous armour, and when the Trojans saw it, they cried out in fear, sure that Achilles had come back. Patroclus drove them back from the ships in a great charge, and for a while the Greeks dared to hope.

image.note: Patroclus in Achilles' armour, Trojans falling back

pages.text: But Patroclus went too far, chasing the Trojans right up to the walls of Troy. There, in the crush of battle, Hector met him, and struck him down. The armour of Achilles was lost, and his dearest friend with it. The news raced back across the field to the ships.

image.note: The tide of battle turning, Hector triumphant

pages.text: When Achilles heard, he fell to the ground, and his cry of grief was so terrible that his goddess mother heard it far beneath the sea. All his anger at Agamemnon was swept away by a far greater one. Now he wanted only one thing: to face Hector, who had killed his friend.

image.note: Achilles overcome with grief in the sand

pages.text: His mother brought him new armour, made by the god of the forge, a shield covered with the whole world in pictures, blazing like fire. Achilles put it on. His quarrel with the Greeks was over. He would fight again, but not for them, and not for glory. He would fight for Patroclus.

image.note: Achilles in god-forged armour, shield gleaming

pages.text: Achilles swept onto the field like a storm, and the Trojans fled before him behind their walls, all but one. Hector alone stayed outside the gate. His parents called down, begging him to come in to safety. But Hector would not hide while his people watched.

image.note: Hector alone before the gates, Achilles nearing

pages.text: Yet when Achilles came on, terrible and shining, even brave Hector's courage shook, and for a while he ran, and Achilles chased him round the walls of the city. At last Hector turned and faced him, for he would rather fall fighting than be caught in flight.

image.note: The chase around the walls of Troy

pages.text: They fought, the two greatest warriors of the war, and Achilles, filled with grief and fury, was too strong. Hector fell. And in his rage Achilles would not even give the body back, but bore it away to the ships, while all Troy wept upon the walls.

image.note: Troy grieving on the walls, distant and restrained

pages.text: That night, an old man came alone through the dark to the Greek camp, to the tent of the very man who had killed his son. It was Priam, the aged king of Troy, Hector's father. He had come, unarmed and unguarded, to beg for his son's body.

image.note: Old King Priam entering Achilles' tent

pages.text: Priam knelt before Achilles and took his hands. "Think of your own father," he said, "who longs for you far away. Have pity on me, who has lost the best of all my sons. Give me back my boy, that I may bury him." And he wept.

image.note: Priam kneeling, Achilles listening

pages.text: And something broke in Achilles, and melted. He thought of his own father, and of Patroclus, and of all the grief of the long war, and he wept too, with the old king, enemy beside enemy. Then, gently, he raised Priam up, and agreed to give Hector back.

image.note: Achilles and Priam weeping together

pages.text: So the anger of Achilles, which had begun the whole sorrow, ended at last in mercy. Hector was carried home, and Troy mourned its hero. Here Homer's tale of the wrath closes, not with a victory, but with two enemies weeping, and one act of kindness in the middle of a terrible war.

image.note: Hector borne home to Troy

pages.text: The war went on after this, and Troy did fall in the end, tricked by a great wooden horse. But that comes in another story. Homer's Iliad is not really about the city at all. It is about anger, and friendship, and grief, and the mercy that even enemies can find.

image.note: The walls of Troy at dusk

pages.text: People to remember. Achilles: the greatest Greek warrior. Hector: the noble champion of Troy. Patroclus: Achilles' dearest friend. Andromache: Hector's wife. Priam: the old king of Troy, and a grieving father.
